title: Three Little Words That Show Students You Care https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/12/16/three-little-words-that-show-students-you-care/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recommends a simple, direct gesture to complement the indirect ways teachers already show care through consistency and kindness: pausing to look an individual student in the eye and sincerely ask, "How are you?" He stresses that the question must be earnest and unhurried rather than a passing throwaway line, since insincerity strips it of meaning while genuine attention can touch a student deeply, particularly because so few adults ever really ask them. He offers variations on the phrase and notes that the specific student response matters far less than the fact that the question was asked at all, since it can be followed with an offer of help that students rarely take up but nonetheless appreciate. He identifies the strategy as especially powerful with difficult students who have mostly experienced negative or manipulative interactions with adults, recommending it be repeated every couple of weeks rather than tracked as a formal checklist obligation.
points: A sincere, unhurried "How are you?" is presented as a simple but powerful direct expression of care, distinct from indirect traits like kindness and consistency.
Insincerity strips the question of meaning; it must involve pausing and genuinely looking at the student, not a passing throwaway line.
The student's specific response matters less than the fact that the question was asked sincerely at all.
The strategy is described as especially effective with difficult students who have mostly experienced negative or manipulative adult interactions.
The gesture should be repeated periodically as a natural habit rather than tracked formally as a checklist task.
quotes: It’s to look individual students in the eye and utter three little words: “How are you?
Now, it’s important to note that it can’t be an off-handed, throwaway line as you’re walking by.
You have to pause the moment. You have to stop what you’re doing, shove aside whatever else is on your mind, and really look at the student. Be present.
It tells them that you’re interested in them as a person, that they’re not just a test score, a face in the crowd, or another cog in the educational machine.
The strategy—if you can call it that—is especially effective with difficult students or those who you’ve had a harder time building a relationship.
It’s just a reminder to touch base. To connect with your students as people.
